newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese government asks for Red Army case report.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese government asks for Red Army case report.

text.p: The Lebanese government said it had asked the justice and interior ministers for full reports on the case of suspected Japanese Red Army guerrillas reported held in Beirut whom Japan wants to extradite.

Beirut newspapers, which have expressed frustration at the confusion over the case and have asked whether the detainees exist or not, poked fun at the announcement, saying the government had asked itself for a report as a delaying tactic.

The conservative daily an-Nahar said the request at a Wednesday night cabinet meeting to Interior Minister Michel al-Murr and Justice Minister Bahij Tabbara looked like a government attempt to gain time while it worked out a way to get out of an embarrassing situation.
Another newspaper, the leftist daily as-Safir, said the focus in the case was moving towards Syria, which has 35,000 troops in Lebanon and is the country's main power broker.

"Japan has opened direct channels with Damascus concerning the latest developments, which means according to observers that things are moving in the direction of a quiet solution," as-Safir said, quoting sources in the Beirut foreign ministry.
Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri was simultaneously quoted as saying Lebanon wanted to maintain good relations with Japan, indicating that Beirut had a lot to lose if it did not.

Hariri pointed out to reporters on Wednesday that Japan pledged at a Friends of Lebanon donors conference in Washington last December to help Lebanon's postwar reconstruction drive. He said a large number of Japanese experts were due to come to Beirut to study projects to which Tokyo could contribute.
He gave no information about the Red Army case but told reporters to await the results of a judicial enquiry which he said was under way.

Murr and Lebanese security sources caused surprise in Beirut earlier this week by saying no Lebanese security or military intelligence agency was holding any Japanese detainees. Judicial sources simultaneously said they were sure that Syrian troops were not holding the Japanese.

Murr's statement contradicted a February 18 statement in Tokyo by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Lebanese officials had told him up to six Red Army suspects had been arrested in the eastern Bekaa Valley.
There has been no public explanation for the confusion, and frustrated Beirut newspapers have asked whether the government is fully in charge of the case.

Lebanese officials have been tight-lipped since Hashimoto's statement, apart from Foreign Minister Faris Bouez who said publicly on the same day that arrests of Japanese Red Army members had taken place.
Other political sources also told Reuters last week the arrests had taken place, but Prosecutor General Adnan Addoum has refused to confirm or deny it.

However, apartment bloc residents in west Beirut told Reuters they saw two Asians -- whom they identified from newspaper photographs as among the Japanese Red Army suspects -- being taken away from their apartment by armed men in plain clothes at five a.m. on February 15.
